newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia welcomes release by U.S. of ex-spy.
newsitem.headline: Russia welcomes release by U.S. of ex-spy.

text.p: Russia on Friday welcomed the release of an ex-KGB agent held in the United States on espionage charges, saying his arrest had been a "crude and provocative" gesture.

The U.S. dismissed its case against Vladimir Galkin on Thursday after Moscow, which accused Washington of violating an unwritten code of behaviour on the treatment of ex-spies, threatened retaliatory measures.
Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), successor organisation to the communist-era KGB, praised the decision, which it said had brought the case to a close.
But it made clear its displeasure at the incident, which it said had damaged friendly relations between the two countries' intelligence services.

"We think that what happened yesterday was sensible and came about through the efforts of the SVR and the foreign ministry and mass media and with great support from Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin," SVR spokeswoman Tatyana Samolis told Reuters.

The 50-year-old former agent, who had not hidden his former occupation on his visa application, was arrested at the airport in New York on October 29 and accused of trying to obtain secret information on the Star Wars programme in 1991.
Chernomyrdin raised his case in a telephone conversation with U.S. Vice President Al Gore on Thursday, appealing to him to limit damage to relations between Washington and Moscow.

A court in Worcester, Massachusetts later dropped the charges against Galkin and the U.S. Justice Department issued a statement saying that the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) had recommended the move in the national interest.
Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) said it had drawn up a concrete list of U.S. candidates for arrest in Russia if the Americans had not let Galkin go.

FSB director Nikolai Kovalyov told Itar-Tass news agency he had stopped all preparations for the arrests after Chernomyrdin's conversation with Gore, in which he said an agreement had been reached on resolving the conflict.
"Now we can consider the case closed," Samolis said, but added that the service would be going over the events in the next few days to try to understand what had been behind them.

"We could have worked this out at the beginning but over two weeks there was no willingness on the part of the FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) to do anything and so the issue became political," she said.

"On our side we can only guess at the reasons behind it. There could be a political motive, a political gesture linked to the U.S. presidential election, or the FBI wanted to show off its professionalism," Samolis said.
"If that is the case then they made a big mistake," she said. "It was a crude and provocative gesture."
SVR first deputy director Alexei Shcherbakov said the U.S. move satisfied Russia's demands on the whole, although it meant that Washington had got out of issuing an apology.

"The SVR will not insist on this part of its demands although we stick to our view that the incident was the crudest provocation, damaging the partnership between the SVR and the CIA," Tass quoted Shcherbakov as saying.
The fair-haired Galkin, dressed in a prison uniform, smiled slightly when he heard the decision of the court in Worcester to drop the charges.
He told reporters his arrest had been a mistake and said he did not know who was responsible, but said later that the FBI had tried to recruit him.

"I was told: Mr Galkin we offer you two ways. One is cooperation with the FBI and an excellent life in America, and the other is seven to ten years of imprisonment for espionage. I chose the second way," he told Itar-Tass news agency.
There was no immediate comment from the FBI.
